variants: So. You have come to fight me. How refreshing - most of my enemies prefer to wait behind their walls until I have finished with the countryside.
Welcome to my field. I say mine; I have not signed anything. I simply find that fields tend to become mine after a while.
You have won. I am almost pleased; a man learns nothing from beating fools. I shall learn from you, and I promise you will not enjoy the lesson.
Beaten, on this ground, today. Note the qualifications. I have made a career of the ground and the day after.
There it is. You came straight at me, like a bull at a red cloak, and now you are wondering where the cloak went.
Finished. You fought like a wall - solid, honest, and completely unable to turn around.
First blood. Good. I was beginning to worry you were one of those enemies who negotiate.
I am coming for you. Not from where you are looking. I never come from where you are looking.
My columns are moving. Watch the front, by all means; someone should, and it may as well be you.
Forward. If it seems too easy, that is because it is meant to.
You are at my camp. A camp is a tent with ambition; I have left better ones to wolves.
Hitting my walls, are you. Every man you spend there is one I need not outwit later.
Take the camp. I have taken cities and given them back; the joy is in the taking, not the holding.
One camp lost. I have lost an eye, an army and a brother, and here I still am.
That camp is mine. I did not even need the elephants. I am almost disappointed.
Your camp changes masters. They will find me a lenient landlord and a very poor tenant.
Your men are falling in rows. That is what happens when you fight a wall's war against a river.
Look at your line. Brave, disciplined, and in exactly the wrong place. Rome taught you well.
My men are dying. Good men, too. The enemy may take them; the enemy may not have my attention as well.
More of mine are coming down the road. I know - I did not tell you. That was rather the idea.
Reinforcements. Mine, I am afraid. I collect them the way others collect debts.
Your commander has fallen. A pity. I had a speech prepared for after, and he would have hated it.
So it ends with a blade after all. Tell Rome I was a wolf, not a bull. She never did learn the difference.
I am nearly done, they say. I have crossed mountains on nearly. Do not count what is left of me; count what it is still holding.
Together, then. I will do the clever part. You may do the brave part; it is honest work and someone must.
Won. Neatly. Remember that half of it was the ground and the other half was the timing, and none of it was luck.
Lost. We fought their war instead of ours. Next time we choose the field before we choose the fight.
My camp is under attack. I would prefer not to be the one caught in a trap for once; if you can help, now would be poetic.
They are at my walls. I have been the hammer so often that I forget what the anvil feels like. It is unpleasant.
I am losing men. Not to cleverness, to weight. Lend me some of yours, or a distraction, or both.
This is the edge. I have stood on it before and walked back. I would rather not do it alone.
That is the end of my army. Not of me - never that - but the war is in your hands now. Turn it.
I am moving on them. Do not follow me directly; be where they run to.
My columns advance. Watch their reserve. It will move when they see me, and that is when it is yours.
That camp is ours. I took it from the side nobody guards, which is every side, eventually.
Your commander is down. Their moment of joy is your moment of opportunity; nobody watches the flanks while they cheer.
